info.bio:
The Strokes es una banda de rock formada en Nueva York, Estados Unidos por Julian Casablancas (vocalista y compositor), Nick Valensi (guitarra principal), Albert Hammond, Jr. (guitarra rítmica), Nikolai Fraiture (bajo) y Fabrizio Moretti (batería) en 1998. Alcanzaron la fama a principios del año 2000 como un grupo líder en la reactivación del garage rock.

Tras el lanzamiento de su aclamado álbum debut Is This It en 2001, muchos críticos nombraron al grupo como los "salvadores del rock"

podcast.title: Formation and Early Work (1998 onwards)
podcast.body: The Strokes, described as an indie band of "trust fund kids" from New York, began performing in the Lower East Side in 1998, developing a set of approximately a dozen songs that garnered attention from "hipsters." "Turns out there was an indie band in New York, made up of some trust fund kids, who were getting the hipsters all in a lather. They'd been knocking around the lower east side, starting in 1998, eventually working up a set of about a dozen songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dual Cover Art for "Is This It" (2001)
podcast.body: The Strokes' 2001 debut album, "Is This It," was released with two distinct covers. The North American version showcased a scientific image of subatomic particles in a bubble chamber, an image previously seen on Prince's "Graffiti Bridge" and a book by Freeman Dyson. The international version, which initially appeared on early North American editions (July and August 2001) before a change, featured a controversial shot of photographer Colin Lane's then-girlfriend's naked rear and hip, wearing a black Chanel glove. "Record collectors will often look for an album that has different covers in different countries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Fierce Bidding War (2001)
podcast.body: The release and popularity of *The Modern Age* EP triggered "the biggest and most fierce bidding war" seen for a rock band in a long time among North American labels. "Meanwhile, a bidding war broke out amongst North American labels. In fact, this was the biggest and most fierce bidding war that we'd seen for a rock band in a long, long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reason for North American Cover Change (2001)
podcast.body: The decision to use the scientific bubble chamber image for the North American cover of "Is This It" was made by The Strokes themselves, as they found it "a lot cooler" than the international nude shot. However, by the time singer Julian Casablancas contacted the label, the first edition of the album had already been pressed with the international cover. Consequently, buyers in North America during July and August 2001 received the original cover before the bubble chamber shot became standard. "When the band stumbled on the bubble chamber picture, they just thought it was a lot cooler and they wanted it to be the cover of the album for the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Albert Hammond Jr. Solo Projects
podcast.body: Albert Hammond Jr. has released a substantial amount of solo material, including four solo records and an EP. "And then we have Albert Hammond Jr., who released four solo records at an EP."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Albert Hammond Jr.'s Background and Role
podcast.body: Albert Hammond Jr. is the son of Albert Hammond Sr., a successful songwriter who wrote songs for artists like Celine Dion, Aretha Franklin, Whitney Houston, Willie Nelson, Chicago, and The Carpenters, and had a writing credit on Radiohead's "Creep." In the early days of The Strokes, Albert was the band's business guy, booking gigs and pitching record companies under the pseudonym "Paul Spencer" (from his fake ID). He collected rejection letters by posting them on a wall. Crucially, he had a credit card funded by his father, which paid for essential band expenses like guitar strings, cables, drumsticks, and rehearsal PA. "Albert was the business guy of the band in the early days. He was the guy who booked gigs and pitch record companies, usually under the pseudonym Paul Spencer, which was the name he used on his old fake ID."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Albert Hammond Jr.'s Drug Problem
podcast.body: During the period leading up to the "Angles" album, Albert Hammond Jr. developed a severe drug problem stemming from a breakup. He used heroin, cocaine, and ketamine, described as "a mess," and required time in rehab to address his addiction. "Another thing, Albert Hammond Jr. had developed a nasty drug problem from a breakup and required time in rehab."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Albert Hammond Jr.'s Fashion Line
podcast.body: Albert Hammond Jr. developed a significant interest in fashion. He launched his own line of men's suits and ties, with a particular enjoyment for designing ties. "He even has his own line of men's suits and ties. He really likes designing ties."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Albert Hammond Jr.'s Solo Trajectory
podcast.body: Following The Strokes' dissolution, Albert Hammond Jr. embarked on a successful solo career with The Voidz, maintaining a positive musical trajectory. This shows a path for individual members after a band's breakup. "Albert Jamon Jr. ha ido haciendo algo muy correcto."

podcast.title: Attention vs. Sales Discrepancy
podcast.body: The Strokes receive a lot of attention, but this has not translated into the high music sales and concert attendance figures typically associated with the biggest bands from the 1970s, 80s, and 90s. "But that hasn't translated into the kind of music sales and concert attendance that we used to see with the biggest bands of all time, the Heritage Acts from the 70s, 80s and 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

podcast.title: Band Formation and Early Members
podcast.body: Julian Casablancas and Nikolai Fraiture met at age six while attending a prestigious French school in New York City. Julian met Albert Hammond Jr. at the Institute Le Rose, a highly expensive private boarding school in Switzerland. By 1997, Julian and Nick Valensi were at Dwight School, where they met Fabrizio Moretti and started a band. Albert moved from Switzerland to New York for film school, became Julian's roommate, and joined the band, with Nikolai joining shortly after as the bassist. "By 1997, Julian and Nick were attending a college prep school called the Dwight School. Again, not cheap."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The band played their first gig under the name The Strokes on September 14, 1999, at The Spiral in New York. The name "The Strokes" has no special story; Julian Casablancas blurted it out during rehearsal, and the group adopted it because it was the name everyone hated the least. "There's no special story behind the name, The Strokes. It's just one that everybody hated the least."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Booker Becomes Manager
podcast.body: The band's performances at small venues, including the Mercury Lounge (capacity 250), greatly impressed the venue's booker. He was so taken with their set of "a little more than a dozen songs" that he quit his job to become The Strokes' manager. "They had a set of a little more than a dozen songs, which so impressed the booker at the Mercury Lounge that he quit and became their manager."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Catalyst for Indie Rock Revolution
podcast.body: The Strokes, through their press, chart success, and radio airplay, acted as a catalyst that "lift[ed] all indie boats," drawing significant attention to the parallel universe of independent acts and labels, akin to the early days of Grunge. "After the stroke started getting press and chart numbers and radio airplay, the tie-in started to lift all indie boats. Just like we saw ten years earlier in the budding days of Grunge, everyone started to look at this parallel universe of independent acts and labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaborator with Sean Lennon
podcast.body: Albert Hammond Jr., a member of The Strokes, worked with Sean Lennon on musical projects. "Albert Hammond Jr. of the Strokes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Concert Attendance Limitations
podcast.body: While The Strokes can attract big crowds, they likely cannot fill an arena or a stadium on their own. "Well, the strokes can attract big crowds. Can they fill an arena or a stadium? Yeah, probably not."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

podcast.title: Continued Reverence
podcast.body: As pioneers of the early 2000s indie rock revival centered in New York, The Strokes maintain a revered status among fans and critics, testament to their lasting influence on guitar-based rock music. "The strokes continued to be revered."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 9: (20-11)

podcast.title: Decline into Self-Caricature and Dissolution
podcast.body: The band fell into a difficult situation, almost becoming a caricature of themselves, with members still performing songs from their first album at 40 years old, which was deemed illogical. This ultimately led to their dissolution, a decision that was not considered a bad one given their trajectory. "La propia banda había caído, pues en una difícil situación casi de una caricatura de ellos mismos, ya tenían 40 años y estar cantando el primer disco de Strokes en las Nights y todo esto con 40 años, pues era una situación no muy lógica y al final ha acabado disolviendo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Defenders of the Cassette
podcast.body: The Strokes are identified as fervent defenders of the cassette tape, actively incorporating its distinctive sound characteristics into their music production, particularly for their first album. This demonstrates their artistic appreciation for the format beyond its technical specifications, embracing its nostalgic and stylistic qualities. "Tenemos bandas como Sony Juzo, como los Strokes, que son unos aferimos defensores de la cinta de cassette."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Distinct Personalities and Spin Magazine Covers
podcast.body: The Strokes' lineup, which has never changed, was noted for its five members having five distinct personalities and images. This individuality was so strong that Spin Magazine eventually featured each member on their own cover. "We had five guys with five distinct personalities and five distinct images. This individuality was so strong that Spin Magazine would eventually give each guy their own cover."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 2000s New York Scene
podcast.body: The Strokes were part of the "new retro garage rock" scene in New York during the early 2000s. "salían en esa época del nuevo rock retro garajero en el yorquino, el que teníamos, pues gente como los Strokes, Long Wave o de Nacional."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Interpol, tras las influencias de la banda

podcast.title: Early Struggles and Financial Support
podcast.body: In the late 90s, the New York rock scene was considered dead, with few venues beyond private parties in Brooklyn warehouses. The Strokes worked through these challenges with Albert Hammond Jr.'s father's credit card and part-time jobs. Julian Casablancas was a bartender at Max's Kansas City, Nikolai Fraiture worked at a video store, Fabrizio Moretti made smoothies, and Albert Hammond Jr. worked at Kim's video. "Along with Albert's dad's credit card, they also had part-time jobs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Embracing Cheap Instruments
podcast.body: The Strokes are cited as a band from the 21st-century indie revival that consciously utilized cheap instruments to cultivate an anti-establishment image. This preference indicated a departure from the traditional pursuit of high-priced vintage guitars. "They wouldn't be caught dead playing, let's say a vintage-less paw, think white stripes, yeah, yeah, yeah, and the strokes and the black keys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

podcast.title: Fabrizio Moretti Solo Projects
podcast.body: Fabrizio Moretti has been involved with several other bands, including Little Joy, Megapus, and Machine Gum. He has also contributed as a helper or session musician with various other artists. "And finally, for Brizio, his worked in bands called Little Joy, Megapus, and Machine Gum, as well as helping out or sitting in with other artists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fabrizio Moretti's Art and Relationships
podcast.body: Fabrizio Moretti works in sculpture and performance art. He was in a relationship with Drew Barrymore for several years, which ended in 2007. "Fabio Moretti works with sculpture and performance arts. He was the one with Drew Barrymore for years, with that ended in 2007."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fabrizio Moretti's Background
podcast.body: Fabrizio Moretti was born in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. His father was a nuclear engineer who relocated the family to New York City. "And drummer for Brizio Mareti was born in Rio de Janeiro. His dad was a nuclear engineer who relocated the family to New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Impressions of Earth Hiatus
podcast.body: The relatively weak commercial and critical performance of the album "First Impressions of Earth" prompted the band to rethink their approach, leading to a three-year break. The tour for this album concluded in 2007, and no new music from The Strokes was released until 2010, marking a five-year gap between albums. "The relatively weak performance of First Impressions of Earth prompted a rethink that lasted three years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Garage Rock Approach
podcast.body: Their music was characterized as a form of Garage Rock, offering a fresh take on a back-to-basics approach previously seen with punk in the 70s and grunge in the early 90s. "They characterized what they were doing as a form of Garage Rock, a fresh take on the same back-to-basics approach that we saw with punk in the 70s and Grunge in the early 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indie Brilliance in Adrift Alt Rock (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: During a period in the early 2000s when Alt Rock was described as "adrift" and lacking new stars, The Strokes were cited as an example of "indie brilliance." "Outside the occasional burst of indie brilliance, you know, the strokes and the white stripes and bands like that, things all really did sound the same for a few years and no real stars emerged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indie Rock Revival (2000s)
podcast.body: The Strokes are listed among the "fresh sounding bands" that played a pivotal role in the Indie Rock Revival of the early 2000s, a period that invigorated interest in new musical styles.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indie Rock Revival Post 9/11
podcast.body: The Strokes were among the bands that drove an indie rock revival following the world events of 9/11 and the American invasion of Iraq and Afghanistan, contributing to a period when rock music began to rise in popularity again. "After 9-11 and the American invasion of Iraq and Afghanistan, Happy music no longer seemed appropriate. This popularity began to rise again, driven by an indie rock revival. I don't think the strokes and the A.A.S and the white stripes and the killers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Influence on Matt Helders
podcast.body: Matt Helders, the drummer for Arctic Monkeys, formed "new allegiances" to The Strokes as he gravitated towards guitar-based indie bands.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Other Bands
podcast.body: The Strokes, particularly with their debut album "Is This It," profoundly influenced many bands that followed, making them one of the most important bands of the 2000s. Kings of Leon learned to play by emulating "Is This It." The Killers, after hearing the album, reportedly scrapped all their existing material except for "Mr. Brightside" and restarted, with elements of The Strokes' construction and recording audible in their music. Other bands like Arctic Monkeys, Franz Ferdinand, and LCD Sound System also credit The Strokes as an influence. "If it wasn't for the Strokes, it's possible that the Indy Rock Garage Rock Revival that took hold in New York City in the early 2000s wouldn't have grown the way it did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Instigators of Rock Revival
podcast.body: The emergence of The Strokes initiated a global resurgence of Rock Revival culture, characterized by a punk influence. They were primarily responsible for a new wave of rock music that generated high demand but had limited offerings at the time. "con el nacimiento de los strokes aparece todo un resorgir de toda la cultura del Rock Rebaival, un poco punk en todo el mundo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Intentional Sound Degradation
podcast.body: The Strokes, like many bands, intentionally used cassette tapes to degrade the sound quality of their recordings. This was done to adapt their sonic aesthetic to the characteristic sound reproduction of the cassette format. "muchas bandas como fueron los strokes o como fueron los white stripes usaban las cintas de caset para degradar la calidad de sonido y adaptar su sonido al sonido que reproducía el caset."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Coleccionar Cassettes. Cosas que hay que saber.

podcast.title: Is This It Album Title and Covers
podcast.body: The band's debut album was titled "Is This It," intentionally without a question mark because it was felt that "it looked wrong." The album featured two different covers. The original cover depicted the photographer's naked girlfriend, fresh out of the shower, with a black glove as a prop, creating a "spinal tapish" effect. Julian Casablancas later suggested a second cover, an image of subatomic particles from a physics experiment at CERN in Switzerland, which was adopted due to label concerns about displaying the naked woman in stores, particularly in the "puritanical US." Releases in July and August 2001 featured the original cover, while all subsequent releases used the second. "No question mark because it was felt that it looked wrong."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Julian Casablancas Solo Projects
podcast.body: Julian Casablancas has released solo records under his own name. Additionally, he formed and released two albums with a band called The Voids. "Julian has won under his own name and two with a band he called The Voids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Julian Casablancas' Background
podcast.body: Julian is the son of John Casablancas, founder of the Elite Model Management Agency, which managed stars like Cindy Crawford, Stephanie Seymour, Gisele Bündchen, Linda Evangelista, Naomi Campbell, Kendall Jenner, Pauline Apport's Gova, Claudia Schiffer, and Heidi Klum. His mother, a former Miss Denmark, encouraged his interest in bands like The Doors, moving him away from Phil Collins records. Julian had a teenage drinking problem, leading him to rehab in high school, which he attributed to his environment, rebelling to be closer to his father. The connection to the modeling agency proved useful, as models from Elite would attend early Strokes gigs, helping with attendance. "He's the son of John Casablanca's, the founder of the famous Elite Model Management Agency."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Julian Casablancas' Folding Electric Bicycle Patent
podcast.body: In the fall of 2015, Julian Casablancas filed for a patent for a folding electric bicycle that did not have pedals. The patent listed Richard Priest, The Strokes' tour manager, and Warren Foo, their video director, as co-inventors alongside Casablancas. "In the fall of 2015, Julian filed for a patent for a folding electric bicycle. No pedals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Julian Casablancas' Privileged Background
podcast.body: Julian Casablancas is the son of the founder of Elite Model Management, one of the world's most important modeling agencies, and Miss Venezuela. He grew up in New York. "A Yulia en el Casablaca se sijo del fundador de élite o la fundada de las agencias de modelo más importantes del mundo y es hijo de mis Venezuela."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Julian Casablancas' Youth and Early Connections
podcast.body: Julian Casablancas, who grew up in New York, was sent to a boarding school in Switzerland due to behavioral issues, where he met "the other guitarist" who would later become a band member. "se tuvo que ir a un interrano suiza porque se portaba muy mal donde conocía lo otro guitarrista."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: The Strokes: Is this it y su portada censurada.

podcast.title: Lack of American Label Interest
podcast.body: Initially, no American record label showed interest in The Strokes. This was attributed to major labels making significant profits from pop acts, diverting all their attention and money to that genre. "It was cool stuff, but no American record label was interested."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Later Stage Performance
podcast.body: The later stage of The Strokes is implicitly contrasted with Julian Casablancas' more successful work with The Voidz. "la última etapa de los Strokes."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Record Store Day 2018. Resumen de lanzamientos.

podcast.title: Limited Chart Success for Albums
podcast.body: Despite being highly acclaimed and influential, only two of The Strokes' albums have ever reached the number one spot on a national album chart, once in the UK and once in Australia. "On only two occasions has one of their albums reached the number one spot on a national album chart, once in the UK and once in Australia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

podcast.title: Lower East Side Gigs
podcast.body: After forming, The Strokes began playing gigs on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, specifically at venues such as the Luna Lounge and the Mercury Lounge. "Eventually, everybody made it back to New York, formed the Strokes, and started playing gigs on the lower east side of Manhattan, specifically at a place called the Luna Lounge, and at another venue called the Mercury Lounge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Modern "New Wave" Application for Rock Revival
podcast.body: In the United States, the term "New Wave" was also extensively used to refer to a new interpretation of Rock Revival music, with The Strokes being one of the bands cited as an example. This highlights the term's adaptability for describing contemporary artists reinterpreting classic rock sounds. "también se le llamó muchísimo New Wave en Estados Unidos a la nueva reinterpretación del Rock River, pues que cienos gente como los Stroves o que hicieron los White Strives."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Move to England for Opportunity
podcast.body: Following in the footsteps of bands like Nirvana, the Pixies, and the Ramones, The Strokes took their act to England, where they received a much warmer welcome and found a label willing to release their music. "So the strokes did what Nirvana and the Pixies had done a dozen years earlier, and what the Ramones did a dozen years before that. They took their act to England, where they received a much warmer welcome."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mystery Model on "Is This It" Cover
podcast.body: The woman featured on the international cover of The Strokes' "Is This It," depicted from behind with a black glove, was the then-girlfriend of photographer Colin Lane. Lane took the spontaneous shot as she stepped out of the shower, utilizing a Chanel glove from a previous shoot. Despite the image's widespread recognition, Lane has never publicly revealed her name, and the couple are no longer together. "Oh, and who is the woman in that photo? No idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: New Wave of Alt-Rock
podcast.body: The Strokes were part of a new crop of indie artists who emerged after the alt-rock bottomed out, many of whom operated outside the standard music industry model, signaling a return for alt-rock in a few years. "They had names like The Arctic Monkeys, Arcade Fire, The White Stripes, The Killers, and The Strokes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Origin, UK/Europe Acceptance
podcast.body: Formed in New York, The Strokes first found acceptance and embrace in the UK and Europe before making a significant impact in their home country. "The Strokes formed in New York but first embraced in the UK and Europe."

podcast.title: New York Origins (Upper West Side)
podcast.body: The Strokes originated from three "preppy kids" on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, Julian Casablancus, Nick Valenci, and Fabio Moretti, all sons of affluent parents. Julian later met Albert Hammond Jr. at a private boarding school in Switzerland. "They start with three preppy kids on the upper west side of Manhattan, sons of rich parents."

podcast.title: Nicholas Valensi's Background
podcast.body: Nicholas Valensi, another member from the Upper East Side of New York, spent his summers on his grandfather's estate in Bordeaux. "Guitarist Nicholas Valenci was another kid from the Upper East Side of New York, who spent his summers on his grandfather's estate in Bordeaux."

podcast.title: Nikolai Fraiture Backstage Incident
podcast.body: During an early show where The Strokes opened for Girl Harbor at Don Hills, Nikolai Fraiture was caught having sex backstage in the basement and photographed. Girl Harbor then used this photo for a flyer for the next Strokes gig, with the caption, "this is what happened at our last show." "Nik was caught having sex backstage down on the basement and was photographed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nikolai Fraiture Solo Projects
podcast.body: Nikolai Fraiture has pursued solo musical endeavors, including a band named Nicolai. He also fronted another band called Summer Moon, which featured Stephen Perkins, the drummer from Jane's Addiction. Fraiture also collaborates with his brother on a project that merges music with performance art painting. "Nicolai had a band called Nicolai and another called Summer Moon, which featured Jane's addiction drummer Stephen Perkins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nikolai Fraiture's Background
podcast.body: Nikolai was the only member who grew up poor. His father worked as a security guard at Macy's, and his family of five lived in a two-room apartment. "It should be noted that out of all the members, Nikolai was the only one who grew up poor."

podcast.title: North American Label Indifference & UK Interest
podcast.body: Initially, no US labels expressed interest in releasing their material, prompting the band to send a demo to Rough Trade Records in the UK, which then agreed to release their *The Modern Age* EP. "Nobody in the US was interested in releasing their stuff, so they sent a demo to rough trade records in the UK, who agreed to release an EP called The Modern Age."

podcast.body: In terms of overall stature, The Strokes fall short when compared to major acts from previous decades such as U2, Green Day, or Pearl Jam. "But if you compare them in terms of overall stature to a U2 or a green day or a Pearl Jam, they kind of fall short."

podcast.title: Stylistic Title Formatting for "Is This It"
podcast.body: The deliberate omission of a question mark in The Strokes' album title "Is This It" was a conscious stylistic decision made by the art director. This choice was based on the belief that including a question mark simply "didn't look right" with the chosen typography and overall design aesthetic. "That's a stylistic decision. According to the art director, it just didn't look right."

podcast.title: The Modern Age EP and Bidding War
podcast.body: The Strokes recorded a three-track demo in 2000, which was unusually tight for a young group due to their insistence on rehearsing to a click track. This led to "The Modern Age" EP, which sold well and ignited one of the fiercest bidding wars among record labels in a long time. Rough Trade Records (UK) won the bid, prompting label head Geoff Travis to resurrect the label to sign The Strokes. They also secured a deal with RCA, which was amenable to the band's desire to make a music video. "The subsequent EP, the three track, the modern age, not only sold respectively well, but also sparked a bidding war amongst record labels."

podcast.title: Trust Fund Band – Most Members from Wealthy Families, Casablancas Money Bankrolled Early Career
podcast.body: Almost every member of The Strokes came from wealthy backgrounds. Singer Julian Casablancas is the son of John Casablancas, head of the Elite Model Agency, home to Cindy Crawford, Linda Evangelista, Claudia Schiffer, Tyra Banks, Cameron Diaz, and Heidi Klum. Julian attended a private school in Switzerland where he met Albert Hammond Jr., the son of 1970s singer-songwriter Albert Hammond ("It Never Rains in Southern California"). Drummer Fabrizio Moretti's parents sent him to the Dwight School, a Manhattan prep school, where he met Julian and guitarist Nick Valensi — the only relatively modest-background member. Bassist Nikolai Fraiture grew up in a two-bedroom apartment with five relatives but still attended a prestigious bilingual school on the Upper West Side. The Casablancas family money funded the band's early gear and operations. "No wonder so many other bands were jealous."

xref.title: Breakup in 2011
xref.body: The White Stripes officially announced their breakup on February 2, 2011, stating it was for "a myriad of reasons, mostly to preserve what is beautiful and special about the band." The band had an influential run from 1997 through 2011, becoming a major part of the Indy Rock revival of the early 2000s alongside bands like The Strokes and Arctic Monkeys. The reasons for the split included Meg White's introverted nature and desire for a personal life, the end of her marriage to Jack White, and Jack's diverging musical ambitions. Following the breakup, Meg White receded into obscurity, while Jack White continued as a solo performer and music industry figure. "The official breakup announcement came on February 2, 2011."

xref.title: Recovery with Wife's Support
xref.body: Despite a poor prognosis, Edwin recovered with the unwavering support of his wife, Grace Maxwell, who encouraged him to draw and write in notebooks with his left hand, as his right hand was rendered useless by the strokes. "His wife, and this was as close to a saint as you'll find, was there every step of the way. It was her idea to help his recovery by getting Edwin to draw."

xref.body: Stephen Perkins, the drummer for Jane's Addiction, also played drums in Summer Moon, a band fronted by Nikolai Fraiture of The Strokes. "Nicolai had a band called Nicolai and another called Summer Moon, which featured Jane's addiction drummer Stephen Perkins."

xref.title: Strokes' "American Girl" Acknowledgment
xref.body: Tom Petty recounted that The Strokes "took American girl for their song Last Night," and he "saw an interview with him saying where they actually admitted it and that made me laugh out loud." Petty expressed a preference for artists admitting influence rather than malicious theft. "The strokes took American girl for their song last night. And I saw an interview with him saying where they actually admitted it and that made me laugh out loud."

xref.title: Toured with White Stripes and Strokes
xref.body: After renaming themselves from Unitarred to The Ye-Eyes, the band quickly began touring with other prominent Garage Rock revival acts, The White Stripes and The Strokes. "Unitarred was renamed the Ye-Eyes and soon found themselves touring with the White Stripes and the Strux."

xref.title: UK Success and Jack White Co-Production
xref.body: Like The White Stripes and The Strokes, The Von Bondis initially found significant attention in the UK. They toured with The White Stripes and other young Garage Rock bands, and Jack White notably co-produced their first album, "Lack of Communication." "It just like the Stripes in the Strokes, the first territory to pay close attention was the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: US Market Struggles (1990s onward)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip never achieved major stardom in the American market, a phenomenon that has become an area of study. While they have pockets of support, their timing often did not align with prevailing American rock trends. For instance, in the 1990s, American rock was dominated by grunge, then hip hop, and later indie rock (like The Strokes or The White Stripes), none of which perfectly matched the Hip's style. "Why has the tragically hip never been able to break through in the States? While this isn't entirely true, the hip do have pockets of support in America. But unlike Brian Adams or Lannis Morsehsett or Nickelback, it just seems that their timing was off. Their music was great, but whenever they were hot, American rock and roll attitudes were somewhere else. In the 90s, it was grunge, and the hip are not grunge. Then came hip hop. Hip didn't belong there. Then it was Indy Rock and the flavor of the strokes, so the white stripes and the hip didn't really fit in there either."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

"They even had Slash, Duff McKagan and Matt Soren from Guns and Roses and Velvet Revolver appear in their video."
